demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson asks DocuMind no question: it reads the ledger, the caches' records and the alert policies, and no read on this page depends on which store answers. The two windows below are on every page; you can skip both here, or pin acme now and put it back at the end if you want the UI's answers to come from the kit's index while you read. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: The UI and the ledger: where a change lands on your lane
demos.purpose: The Documents page as yourself, the same ledger through the API as the UI's account, then the three records the caches compare. A change ends in the ledger, so read the ledger first, where an operator would. The UI's address is built from your project number, as the setup block built API: Open it signed in to Google as yourself and choose Documents. The Versions table is the ledger: one row per source, with its status, its chunks, what its last change cost (reused, embedded, retired), the embedding it was made with, when it landed and where it is held. The caption above it prints the count of current versions, the corpus fingerprint, the last change and the tenant's data_region. Your email maps to acme, so these are acme's rows. The same rows come from the API. GET /v1/sources is the versions view main.py serves. The shell calls it as documind-ui-sa, the UI's own account, which make roster put on all three tenants, so the call could name any of them. The UI asked as you, and only acme was yours. One ledger, two callers: The same rows come from the API. GET /v1/sources is the versions view main.py serves. The shell calls it as documind-ui-sa, the UI's own account, which make roster put on all three tenants, so the call could name any of them. The UI asked as you, and only acme was yours. One ledger, two callers: any is acme's data_region, set by make roster, and it is why the managed stores hold acme's copies. The handbook row's last three counts are what its last change cost: an undo shows 283 reused and 0 embedded, and a re-issue like revision 2 shows 281 and 2. Then the three records that decide whether a cache may be used. Firestore holds them, and the cell reads each one directly:

demos.heading: Architecture: the path a change takes, station by station
demos.purpose: The cell cuts version 1 and revision 2 of the handbook with shared/documind_corpus.py, the notebooks' twin of the worker's chunker, which mints the same chunk texts and hashes. It applies the carry-over's rule: a chunk is reused when its hash is held. Then it cuts the same two texts as whole-document windows, the way the worker cut a handbook before 12 September 2026.

demos.heading: Failure modes: what pages, what does not, and what the design does about it
demos.purpose: The cell reads every Terraform file, lists the alert policies that watch the document lifecycle with what each one reads and when it exists, and counts the policies that read the main subscription, its oldest unacknowledged age, and cache_stale. The walk's planner is pure Python. The cell hands it three objects nobody indexed: one whose claim was cut off in processing, one zero-byte object, and one PDF the worker queued for the batch lane. Then it asks the claim's lease what the night's rewrite of the first will find. The same list from the Monitoring API: every policy on your lane by name, and whether any of them reads the main subscription or the dead-letter one.
